The '''design of Star Wars CCG''' began in 1995 with [[Tom Braunlich]] and [[Rollie Tesh]], the designers of Decipher's ''Star Trek'' CCG. Braunlich and Tesh wrote the core rules, [[Warren Holland]] approved every card, and [[Jerry Darcy]] led the design of the expansions.<ref name="bp28" /><ref name="rfd14" /><ref name="darcy2020" /> Premiere shipped in December 1995. After Decipher lost the license in 2001, the volunteer [[Players Committee]] took over design and has made virtual cards since 2002.<ref name="rfd-holland" /> Inspirations are covered in [[Inspirations for Star Wars CCG]].

== Origins ==
Braunlich and Tesh, ''Pente'' champions from Tulsa, Oklahoma, had designed Decipher's ''Star Trek: The Next Generation'' CCG.<ref name="rfd14" /><ref name="bp27" /> Braunlich said Decipher "wanted to immediately grab the Star Wars license" before the first ''Star Trek'' sets were finished. He added: "even before the license was completed, we started working on it".<ref name="bp28" /> The two designers moved from the Seattle area to Norfolk, Virginia, to work at Decipher.<ref name="rfd14" /> Darcy has said a mass-market partnership with Parker Brothers helped Decipher win the license; the [[Premiere Two-Player Introductory Game]] came out of that deal.<ref name="darcy-pnh" />

Braunlich and Tesh began with a retreat at the Florida home of game designer Richard Borg and "came back from there with a general plan".<ref name="bp28" /> Braunlich calls the following year "my lost year", with "80, 90 hours a week on the details of these cards".<ref name="bp28" />

== The team ==
Braunlich and Tesh were outside consultants, not Decipher employees.<ref name="darcy2020" /> Tesh described their role: "Tom and I are essentially the conceptualization. I think we come up with the original ideas and then turn those over to people like Bill and Jerry".<ref name="rfd14" /> The Premiere design room was Braunlich, Tesh, Holland, sales and design head Ross Campbell, and Darcy. Sessions ran "from like 10 o'clock in the morning till 2 o'clock in the morning".<ref name="darcy-pnh" /> Art director Dan Burns ran the art department.<ref name="darcy2020" />

Holland had the final word on every card. Braunlich called him "a real taskmaster. He would not let any card go by that he didn't love."<ref name="bp28" /> [[Bill Martinson]], lead designer of the ''Star Trek'' game, edited SWCCG card text with Holland.<ref name="darcy-dag" />

Darcy joined Decipher in 1995 in ''Star Trek'' customer service and moved into design "based on proximity".<ref name="darcy2020" /> He ran the game "unofficially" from ''A New Hope'' and as lead designer from ''Hoth''.<ref name="darcy-pnh" /> In 1999 he described the job: "[[Chuck Kallenbach]], [[Tom Lischke]] and Mike Reynolds will come up with card ideas and I'll tell them what's wrong with them."<ref name="rfd12" /> [[Sandy Wible]] and Darcy were the core design team for ''Dagobah''.<ref name="darcy-dag" /> Lischke, a top tournament player, was hired after ''Hoth'' and acted as "the tournament player's advocate".<ref name="coth13" /> Kallenbach, a playtester since before Premiere, joined Decipher in 1997.<ref name="coth15" /><ref name="tor-kallenbach" /> Braunlich said the design staff grew to "a dozen people".<ref name="bp28" />

== Core mechanics ==
=== The Force and the deck ===
Braunlich called the draw deck as the Force "my big contribution".<ref name="bp28" /> Tesh described how it started: "we started with the idea of each player having a base that you were building up and the opponent was trying to destroy. And then Tom had the idea ... what if it was the deck that represented the base".<ref name="rfd14" /> The deck became the scoring device "because we were wanting the game to be completely self-contained and elegant". Tesh said "the whole concept of the flow of the force grew out of that".<ref name="rfd14" /> The Used Pile and Force Pile took "weeks and weeks" and "a lot of different versions".<ref name="rfd14" />

=== Destiny ===
Braunlich credits Tesh with destiny numbers: cards "drawn from the deck in order to essentially simulate the roll of the dice". Strong cards got low destiny numbers, which Braunlich hoped would "give the people managing the set later on some tools".<ref name="bp28" /> The designers expected that good players might memorize the order of their cards, and decided "if they're that good ... they deserve that advantage".<ref name="rfd14" />

=== Attrition ===
At first battle destiny was simply added to power. Darcy said Braunlich and Tesh then saw that "the person who's the most powerful is just going to keep winning. There's no come from behind element. And so let's add attrition so that even if you win, you lose something".<ref name="darcy-pnh" /> Kallenbach links attrition's complexity to playtesting: weapons were left out of the first tests because "we know they already work".<ref name="coth15" />

=== Force drains ===
Two accounts describe the origin of Force drains. Kallenbach said that at the first in-person playtest, battles at empty sites drained whole decks. Overnight, playtester Mark Tuttle proposed Force icons on both sides of a location to limit the damage, and the group agreed "It's going to balance the game".<ref name="bp07" /> Darcy said he and Tesh hit a stalled test game and "realized we needed a tiebreaker of some kind". He added that "multiple people came to that conclusion".<ref name="darcy-pnh" />

=== Light Side and Dark Side ===
Holland wanted the hero's journey of Joseph Campbell in the game, which "proved to be a little bit too much". The team "decided early on that it had to be light side and dark side and light force and dark force".<ref name="bp28" /> Darcy described the balance: "the dark side is meant to be quicker, easier, more seductive ... But it's a false choice. It presents as more powerful, but it actually isn't."<ref name="darcy-dag" /> Light Side characters had higher forfeit and slightly higher destiny; Dark Side characters had more power and lower deploy costs.<ref name="darcy-dag" />

=== Systems and parsecs ===
When Darcy arrived, systems and sites existed but movement between systems did not. He drew the galaxy map from West End Games' ''Star Wars'' roleplaying game on a blackboard, so that hyperspace moves "would just be a matter of subtraction".<ref name="darcy-pnh" />

== Making the cards ==
=== Card reviews ===
The Premiere team met after hours in Braunlich's apartment and projected "giant images of cards" on the wall. Braunlich proposed card functions, Darcy worked on "the particulars of the numbers", and the group "would incrementally improve each one" until "three or four o'clock in the morning".<ref name="bp28" /> Holland wanted every card to make players "feel like you were holding part of the Star Wars universe".<ref name="bp28" /> There were no balance formulas. Kallenbach said: "Everything was seat of the pants."<ref name="coth15" />

=== Images ===
Decipher bought an original print of ''Star Wars'' and an expensive editing machine to capture frames, and the team "scoured every frame of those movies".<ref name="bp28" /><ref name="ringer" /> Lucasfilm opened its props department at Skywalker Ranch for photographs.<ref name="bp28" /> Background aliens from the cantina became cards. An image was a hard requirement: when Kallenbach proposed a card, Tesh asked "what's the image?"<ref name="coth15" /> Artists spent most of their time removing film grain, and later created images by computer.<ref name="darcy2020" />

=== Lore and Lucasfilm ===
Card lore had to be approved by Lucasfilm. Braunlich said "all of the lore things had to be approved or justified", with notes giving each source, and Darcy handled most of it.<ref name="bp28" /> Lucasfilm let Decipher name unnamed background characters. Darcy recalled the answer: "Can we name it? Knock yourself out."<ref name="darcy2020" /> Decipher drew lore from West End Games' roleplaying books: "From a lore standpoint, we definitely stood on their shoulders."<ref name="darcy2020" /> Kallenbach named some ''Jabba's Palace'' aliens by drawing Scrabble tiles.<ref name="coth15" />

== Playtesting ==
Darcy called early playtesting "by today's standards, shamefully naive".<ref name="darcy-pnh" /> Decipher flew testers to a hotel for a few days of play and brainstorming. "You get one shot to get as much feedback as you can", Darcy said, after which the cards went to the printer.<ref name="darcy-pnh" /> Braunlich said testers "were there to try to break the game".<ref name="bp28" /> Testers received packets of photocopied cards to cut out and play.<ref name="coth15" />

By ''Dagobah'', top tournament players signed NDAs and tested remotely with their own groups.<ref name="darcy-dag" /> Decipher had no full-time testers, which Darcy later called "a absolutely necessary component".<ref name="darcy-dag" /> In 1998 the team said its playtest system was "bigger than it's ever been" and included "three or four current or ex top ten players".<ref name="rfd02" />

== Expansions ==
The team planned expansions from the start. Braunlich said "the seeds of those sets was laid down in the original set", and some icons were printed before their rules existed.<ref name="bp28" /> During Premiere, Darcy wrote the set list on a blackboard: Hoth, Dagobah, Cloud City, Tatooine, Endor, Death Star.<ref name="darcy-pnh" /> Each set drew only on its part of the films, which left ''Dagobah'' with Luke and Yoda as its only Light Side characters.<ref name="darcy-dag" />

Lucasfilm's re-release of the films was a surprise: "we had no idea that George was gonna wanna do special edition".<ref name="coth13" /> ''[[Special Edition]]'' was meant to lift falling sales and gather the rules into "a one-stop shop".<ref name="coth13" /> Its operatives were added late and became a known mistake.<ref name="coth13" /><ref name="coth15" />

=== Rarity ===
Braunlich said "about half of the sales of these games went to collectors", so Decipher wanted strong cards in every set.<ref name="bp28" /> The 1995 team treated rarity as a balancing tool. Darcy later said "that proved false" and that "the extreme rarity of the mains was unfortunately limiting".<ref name="darcy-pnh" /> SWCCG cards had no collector numbers or rarity icons until Decipher added them for ''[[Young Jedi]]''.<ref name="rfd16" />

=== No banned cards ===
Decipher's policy was to fix problem cards, not ban them. In 1998 the designers said the only card Decipher had ever banned was from ''Star Trek'' Premiere: "We want to make sure that every card you have, you can play."<ref name="rfd02" /> Darcy said this was "a passion of Warren's".<ref name="darcy-pnh" /> Braunlich wanted fixes to be "an elegant solution", but said "in the end, there was too much of that".<ref name="bp28" />

== Regrets ==
Darcy said he "utterly failed" his goal of avoiding permission decks such as Sense and Alter. He "spent the rest of my time on that game trying to fix that mistake".<ref name="darcy-pnh" /> He took the blame for creatures and for the capture rules.<ref name="darcy2020" /><ref name="darcy-dag" /> A rule meant to let the Dark Side deploy to Dagobah after a Light Side drain there was lost "in production".<ref name="darcy-dag" /> He also judged that designing for tournament players "in retrospect was a mistake".<ref name="coth13" />

== Players Committee ==
Decipher's planned last product, internally called "Reflections Virtual Gold", included about 100 "virtual cards" with blank game text. A players committee would post the text on the web every four to six months; Lucasfilm turned the plan down.<ref name="rfd-holland" /> In December 2001 Holland announced the [[Players Committee]] to post replacement text for existing cards. He called it "a small body of fans consisting of some of the best players and playtesters in the world".<ref name="rfd-holland" />

The Players Committee's design and development team creates virtual cards, evaluates the meta for errata, and runs iterative playtesting.<ref name="pc-org" /> Designer [[Ryan Jellison]] said the team makes at most about 30 cards a quarter, because proofing, graphics and coding for [[GEMP]] all touch every card.<ref name="jellison" /> Volunteers code cards in Java through a GitHub repository, and some cards need new functions.<ref name="jellison" /> A character's game text is limited to five lines. The team avoids keywords and shorthand and writes rules out in full, as Decipher did.<ref name="jellison" /> Jellison said "every card that we make has a home somewhere", unlike the "common chaff" of Decipher's sets.<ref name="jellison" />
